unmapped_findings: The compressive true stress-strain curve of this material at 500 °C and 0.001 s^-1 peaks near the 550-560 MPa level and shows appreciable flow softening after a true strain of 0.3 (Fig. 1c); note the curve corresponds to the full compression test to true strain 0.6, of which the present sample is the interruption at ε=0.3.

The starting microstructure before deformation is a triplex (ferrite + austenite + thermally induced martensite) obtained by annealing at 950 °C/1 h, with extremely low dislocation density in the ferrite and austenite phases (Fig. 1a-b).

The SEM-EDS compositional partitioning reported in Table 1 (Mn 10.3±0.1 wt% in ferrite vs 12.8±0.1 wt% in austenite; Al 6.0±0.1 wt% in ferrite vs 4.7±0.1 wt% in austenite) is stated for deformation at 500 °C up to a true strain of 0.6, so it nominally belongs to the ε=0.6 sibling sample rather than this ε=0.3 sample.
The steel has a high stacking fault energy of 80-110 mJ/m^2, which makes the austenite-to-martensite transformation theoretically impossible and rules out a classical TRIP effect.

Deformation-induced ferrite transformation (DIFT) and deformation-induced austenite transformation (DIAT) occur simultaneously at 500 °C (a phenomenon only observed at this low temperature regime and not at 600 °C), acting as an effective strain compensation mechanism.
